questions.text: Which one of the following is NOT necessarily a property of a Group?
questions.optC: Existence of inverse for every element
questions.subject: 1. Discrete Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: A group requires associativity, an identity and an inverse for each element. Commutativity is an additional Abelian-group axiom; a permutation group such as S3 need not satisfy it.

questions.text: What is the chromatic number of an n-vertex simple connected graph which does not contain any odd length cycle? Assume $n \ge 2$.
questions.subject: 1. Discrete Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: A graph with no odd cycle is bipartite, so two colours suffice. Connectedness with at least two vertices ensures an edge, so one colour cannot suffice.

questions.text: Which one of the following is TRUE for any simple connected undirected graph with more than 2 vertices?
questions.optA: No two vertices have the same degree
questions.optB: At least two vertices have the same degree
questions.optC: At least three vertices have the same degree
questions.optD: All vertices have the same degree
questions.subject: 1. Discrete Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: In a connected simple n-vertex graph the degrees lie in 1 through n-1. There are n vertices but only n-1 possible degrees, so the pigeonhole principle forces two equal degrees.

questions.text: Consider the binary relation: R = {(x, y), (x, z), (z, x), (z, y)} on the set {x, y, z}. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.optA: R is symmetric but NOT antisymmetric
questions.optB: R is NOT symmetric but antisymmetric
questions.optC: R is both symmetric and antisymmetric
questions.optD: R is neither symmetric nor antisymmetric
questions.subject: 1. Discrete Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: The pair (x,y) occurs but (y,x) does not, disproving symmetry. Both (x,z) and (z,x) occur with x different from z, disproving antisymmetry.

questions.text: What is the minimum number of gates required to implement the Boolean function $(AB+C)$ if we have to use only 2-input NOR gates?
questions.subject: 9. Digital Logic
questions.referenceAnswer: Write $AB+C=(A+C)(B+C)$. Two NOR gates produce $u=\overline{A+C}$ and $v=\overline{B+C}$; a third gives $\overline{u+v}=(A+C)(B+C)$. Two gates cannot produce this nonconstant three-variable function: an unrepeated NOR cascade gives $XY+\overline Z$, not $XY+Z$.

questions.text: What is the number of swaps required to sort $n$ elements using selection sort, in the worst case?
questions.subject: 7. Algorithms
questions.referenceAnswer: Selection sort performs at most one swap per outer iteration, hence at most $n-1$ swaps. Inputs exist requiring a linear number, giving $\Theta(n)$ swaps even though comparisons are quadratic.

questions.text:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct regarding Bellman-Ford shortest path algorithm?
P. Always finds a negative weighted cycle, if one exists.
Q. Finds whether any negative weighted cycle is reachable from the source
questions.subject: 7. Algorithms
questions.referenceAnswer: A source-initialized Bellman-Ford run detects a negative cycle only if that cycle is reachable from its source: an edge remains relaxable after the usual passes. A negative cycle in an unreachable component leaves all its distances infinite, so P is false and Q is true.

questions.text: Let $\pi_A$ be a problem that belongs to the class NP. Then which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.optA: There is no polynomial time algorithm for $\pi_A$
questions.optB: If $\pi_A$ can be solved deterministically in polynomial time, then $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$
questions.optC: If $\pi_A$ is NP-hard, then it is NP-complete
questions.subject: 7. Algorithms
questions.referenceAnswer: NP membership plus NP-hardness is precisely NP-completeness. An arbitrary NP problem could already lie in P, so solving that particular problem in polynomial time does not by itself establish P=NP. All NP languages are decidable.

questions.text: Which one of the following is FALSE?
questions.optA: There is unique minimal DFA for every regular language
questions.optB: Every NFA can be converted to an equivalent PDA.
questions.optC: Complement of every context-free language is recursive.
questions.optD: Every nondeterministic PDA can be converted to an equivalent deterministic PDA.
questions.subject: 2. TOC
questions.referenceAnswer: Nondeterministic pushdown automata recognize all context-free languages, while deterministic pushdown automata recognize a strict subset. Minimal DFA uniqueness is understood up to state renaming; an NFA is a PDA that ignores its stack, and context-free languages and their complements are decidable.

questions.subject: Software Engineering
questions.text:
The coupling between different modules of a software is categorized as follows:
I. Content coupling
II. Common coupling
III. Control coupling
IV. Stamp coupling
V. Data coupling
Coupling between modules can be ranked in the order of strongest (least desirable) to weakest (most desirable) as follows:
questions.referenceAnswer: Depending on another module's internals is strongest (content), followed by shared global data (common), control flags, a shared composite structure (stamp), and individual data parameters. Thus the five listed categories run I, II, III, IV, V.

questions.text:
An unbalanced dice (with 6 faces, numbered from 1 to 6) is thrown. The probability that the face value is odd is 90% of the probability that the face value is even. The probability of getting any even numbered face is the same.
If the probability that the face is even given that it is greater than 3 is 0.75, which one of the following options is closest to the probability that the face value exceeds 3?
questions.subject: 11. Engg. Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: Let the probability of an even result be $E$. Then $E+0.9E=1$, so $E=10/19$, and each even face has probability $10/57$. The probability of an even face greater than 3 is $20/57$. Hence $P(X>3)=(20/57)/(3/4)=80/171\simeq0.467836$, closest to 0.468.

questions.text: $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}(1-\tan x)/(1+\tan x)\,dx$ evaluates to
questions.subject: 11. Engg. Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: The integrand is $\tan(\pi/4-x)$. With $u=\pi/4-x$, the integral is $\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan u\,du=[-\ln\cos u]_0^{\pi/4}=\tfrac12\ln2$.

questions.text:
Consider the following well-formed formulae:
I. $\neg \forall x(P(x))$
II. $\neg \exists x(P(x))$
III. $\neg \exists x(\neg P(x))$
IV. $\exists x(\neg P(x))$
Which of the above are equivalent?
questions.subject: 1. Discrete Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: Negating a universal quantifier gives an existential quantifier with the predicate negated: $\neg\forall xP(x)\equiv\exists x\neg P(x)$. Thus I and IV are equivalent. II instead means that P is false everywhere, while III means it is true everywhere.

questions.text:
Consider a system with 4 types of resources R1 (3 units), R2 (2 units), R3 (3 units), R4 (2 units). A non-preemptive resource allocation policy is used. At any given instance, a request is not entertained if it cannot be completely satisfied. Three processes P1, P2, P3 request the resources as follows if executed independently.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Process P1:} & \text{Process P2:} & \text{Process P3:} \\ \hline \text{t = 0: requests 2 units of R2} & \text{t = 0: requests 2 units of R3} & \text{t = 0: requests 1 unit of R4} \\ \hline \text{t = 1: requests 1 unit of R3} & \text{t = 2: requests 1 unit of R4} & \text{t = 2: requests 2 units of R1} \\ \hline \text{t = 3: requests 2 units of R1} & \text{t = 4: requests 1 unit of R1} & \text{t = 5: releases 2 units of R1} \\ \hline \text{t = 5: releases 1 unit of R2} & \text{t = 6: releases 1 unit of R3} & \text{t = 7: requests 1 unit of R2} \\ \hline \text{and 1 unit of R1} & \text{t = 8: Finishes} & \text{t = 8: requests 1 unit of R3} \\ \hline \text{t = 7: releases 1 unit of R3} &  & \text{t = 9: Finishes} \\ \hline \text{t = 8: requests 2 units of R4} &  &  \\ \hline \text{t = 10: Finishes} &  &  \\ \hline\end{array}$
Which one of the following statements is TRUE if all three processes run concurrently starting at time $t=0$?
questions.optA: All processes will finish without any deadlock
questions.optB: Only P1 and P2 will be in deadlock
questions.optC: Only P1 and P3 will be in deadlock
questions.optD: All three processes will be in deadlock
questions.subject: 5. Operating Systems
questions.referenceAnswer: P1 can block on its two-unit R1 request while P3 holds two R1 units. P3 subsequently releases both; this enables P1. P2 can obtain the remaining R1 unit, releases R3, and completes, freeing its other holdings. P1 releases a unit of R2, allowing P3's R2 request; sufficient R3 then becomes available for P3 to finish. P3 releases R4 so P1 can finish. Blocking delays the later operations of that process; the finite waits do not form a permanent cycle.

notes: Answer transcribed from the printed Deadlock key, PDF page 3 / book page 563.

questions.text: A multilevel page table is preferred in comparison to a single level page table for translating virtual address to physical address because
questions.optA: it reduces the memory access time to read or write a memory location
questions.optB: it helps to reduce the size of page table needed to implement the virtual address space of a process
questions.optC: it is required by the translation look aside buffer
questions.optD: it helps to reduce the number of page faults in page replacement algorithms.
questions.subject: 5. Operating Systems
questions.referenceAnswer: A multilevel page table allocates lower-level tables only for mapped regions of a sparse virtual address space. It reduces page-table memory use, while an uncached translation may actually need more memory accesses. It is neither a TLB requirement nor a page-replacement improvement.

Which one of the following is NOT the sequence of edges added to the minimum spanning tree using Kruskal's algorithm?

Consider two transactions $T_1$ and $T_2$, and four schedules $S_1$, $S_2$, $S_3$, $S_4$ of $T_1$ and $T_2$ as given below:
$T_1:R_1[x]\ W_1[x]\ W_1[y]$
$T_2:R_2[x]\ R_2[y]\ W_2[y]$
$S_1:R_1[x]\ R_2[x]\ R_2[y]\ W_1[x]\ W_1[y]\ W_2[y]$
$S_2:R_1[x]\ R_2[x]\ R_2[y]\ W_1[x]\ W_2[y]\ W_1[y]$
$S_3:R_1[x]\ W_1[x]\ R_2[x]\ W_1[y]\ R_2[y]\ W_2[y]$
$S_4:R_2[x]\ R_2[y]\ R_1[x]\ W_1[x]\ W_1[y]\ W_2[y]$
Which of the above schedules are conflict-serializable?
questions.subject: 12. DBMS
questions.referenceAnswer: Compare only operations on the SAME data item from different transactions, with at least one write. S1 and S4 have T2 -> T1 from R2[x] before W1[x] and T1 -> T2 from W1[y] before W2[y], so each is cyclic. In S2 all conflicts point T2 -> T1; T1 never conflicts with a T2 write on x because no such write exists. S3 has only T1 -> T2. Thus exactly S2 and S3 are conflict-serializable. An exhaustive same-item conflict audit confirms the printed B key.

questions.text:
In the RSA public key cryptosystem, the private and public keys are $(e,n)$ and $(d,n)$ respectively, where $n=p*q$ and $p$ and $q$ are large primes. Besides, $n$ is public and $p$ and $q$ are private. Let $M$ be an integer such that $0<M<n$ and $\phi(n)=(p-1)(q-1)$. Now consider the following equations.
I. $M'=M^e\bmod n$; $M=(M')^d\bmod n$
II. $ed\equiv1\bmod n$
III. $ed\equiv1\bmod\phi(n)$
IV. $M'=M^e\bmod\phi(n)$; $M=(M')^d\bmod\phi(n)$
Which of the above equations correctly represent RSA cryptosystem?
questions.referenceAnswer: RSA uses arithmetic modulo $n$ for messages and $ed\equiv1\pmod{\phi(n)}$ for inverse exponents. Therefore I and III apply. Congruence modulo n in II is the wrong inverse condition, and reducing messages modulo $\phi(n)$ in IV loses information. The scan calls e private and d public, reversing common variable naming; the inverse-exponent mathematics works in either direction. Euler's theorem for units and CRT for multiples of p or q justify recovery.

issues: Source private/public exponent names e,d reverse a common textbook convention. Source equations and naming retained.

questions.text: Let $G(x)$ be the generator polynomial used for CRC checking. What is the condition that should be satisfied by $G(x)$ to detect odd number of bits in error?
questions.optB: $G(x)$ does not divide $1+x^{k}$, for any $k$ not exceeding the frame length
questions.optD: $G(x)$ has an odd number of terms
questions.subject: 3. Computer Networks
questions.referenceAnswer: For an odd-weight error polynomial E, $E(1)=1$ over GF(2). If G has factor $x+1$, every multiple of G has value zero at 1. Therefore such an E cannot be divisible by G, and the CRC detects every odd number of flipped bits.

I. The cyclomatic complexity of a module is equal to the maximum number of linearly independent circuits in the graph.
II. The cyclomatic complexity of a module is the number of decisions in the module plus one, where a decision is effectively any conditional statement in the module.

questions.referenceAnswer: Manual review: under the usual binary-decision, single-entry/single-exit CFG convention, $V=E-N+2$ is decisions plus one and the number of independent entry-to-exit paths, so II and III give B. A sub-sequence of a given sequence is just the given sequence with some elements (possibly none or all) left out. We are given two sequences $X[m]$ and $Y[n]$ of lengths $m$ and $n$, respectively, with indexes of $X$ and $Y$ starting from 0.
We wish to find the length of the longest common sub-sequence (LCS) of $X[m]$ and $Y[n]$ as $l(m,n)$, where an incomplete recursive definition for the function $l(i,j)$ to compute the length of the LCS of $X[m]$ and $Y[n]$ is given below:
$$l(i,j)=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if either }i=0\text{ or }j=0,\\\mathrm{expr1},&\text{if }i,j>0\text{ and }X[i-1]=Y[j-1],\\\mathrm{expr2},&\text{if }i,j>0\text{ and }X[i-1]\ne Y[j-1].\end{cases}$$
Which one of the following options is correct?
questions.subject: 7. Algorithms
questions.referenceAnswer: For equal last symbols, $l(i,j)=1+l(i-1,j-1)$. For unequal last symbols, drop either final symbol and take the better result: $l(i,j)=\max(l(i-1,j),l(i,j-1))$. Thus expr2 in C is correct; D contains a circular dependency on l(i,j).

$$l(i,j)=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if either }i=0\text{ or }j=0,\\\mathrm{expr1},&\text{if }i,j>0\text{ and }X[i-1]=Y[j-1],\\\mathrm{expr2},&\text{if }i,j>0\text{ and }X[i-1]\ne Y[j-1].\end{cases}$$
The values of $l(i,j)$ could be obtained by dynamic programming based on the correct recursive definition of $l(i,j)$ of the form given above, using an array $L[M,N]$, where $M=m+1$ and $N=n+1$, such that $L[i,j]=l(i,j)$.
Which one of the following statements would be TRUE regarding the dynamic programming solution for the recursive definition of $l(i,j)$?
questions.optA: All elements of $L$ should be initialized to 0 for the values of $l(i,j)$ to be properly computed
questions.optB: The values of $l(i,j)$ may be computed in a row major order or column major order of $L[M,N]$
questions.optC: The values of $l(i,j)$ cannot be computed in either row major order or column major order of $L[M,N]$
questions.optD: $L[p,q]$ needs to be computed before $L[r,s]$ if either $p<r$ or $q<s$

Each remaining cell depends on its top, left and optionally diagonal predecessor; increasing row-major or increasing column-major traversal supplies all of them. D imposes an unjustified ordering even between unrelated cells, such as (0,2) and (1,1).

Statement for Linked Answer Questions 57 and 58:
Frames of $1000$ bits are sent over a $10^{6},\text{bps}$ duplex link between two hosts. The propagation time is $25,\text{ms}$. Frames are to be transmitted into this link to maximally pack them in transit (within the link). What is the minimum number of bits ($l$) that will be required to represent the sequence numbers distinctly? Assume that no time gap needs to be given between transmission of two frames.
questions.subject: 3. Computer Networks
questions.referenceAnswer: A frame takes $1000/10^6=1$ ms to enter the link. The 25 ms propagation interval can contain 25 distinct frames. Therefore $2^l\ge25$, so $l=\lceil\log_2 25\rceil=5$. This is one-way in-transit packing, as the scan explicitly says, rather than full RTT window sizing.
